t: How To Develop Good Listening The First Month Of School nth-of-school/
q: Dwelling on it or complaining about it—as many teachers are wont to do—is a waste of time.
When it comes to developing good listening, the key is to speak in a way that will cause your students to tune in naturally.
Most teachers talk too loud, believing that it helps students pay attention. But the truth is, it does the opposite.
Repeating yourself effectively removes any reason for your students to listen to you the first time.
The fewer words you use, the better your students will listen.
Remembering to pause will give your students a moment to download the previous information.
But good listening isn’t about the students. It’s about the teacher.

t: How To Get Parents On Your Side
q: Which is why it’s critical that you get them on your side, critical that they like you and trust you and support your program.
It’s so powerful, in fact, that it outperforms all other strategies combined.
You make sure your students have a great first day—as well as first week and first month—of school .
Because they know that when their child is happy, they learn. They grow socially and academically.
So when their child leaps into their car smiling from ear to ear and offering a glowing review of their first day or first week, they exhale a summer’s worth of tension.
So instead of having parents in your ear , waiting for you after school, and emailing you in the middle of the night, they merely smile and wave.

t: How To Teach Classroom Management On The First Day Of School he-first-day-of-school/
q: No, you must set your feet, narrow your eyes, and teach classroom management in a way your students won’t soon forget.
Before your students arrive, make an ironclad commitment to yourself to abide by the guidelines set forth in your classroom management plan .
To begin your lesson, make a promise to your students that you will uphold your classroom management plan every minute of every day , no exceptions.
Now promise your students that you will always treat them with respect. Promise that you will never yell, scold, or humiliate them in any way.
Your classroom management plan is the very thing that ensures your students’ freedom to learn and enjoy school without interference.

The lesson is most effective if you pretend to be the misbehaving student. Sit at one of their desks and call out without raising your hand, side-talk with a classmate, or engage in any other common misbehavior.
The idea behind teaching classroom management so thoroughly right out of the gate is to remove any and all excuses for poor behavior before they gain a toehold.

q: It is the initial impression of your classroom, after all, that establishes its culture.
The old maxim that you shouldn’t smile the first two months of the school year is terrible advice.
A genuine smile creates instant likability, builds effortless rapport, and activates the power of reciprocation.
Your calm demeanor alone, without having to say a word, has a powerful effect on students—much more than most teachers realize.
When it comes to effective classroom management, clarity trumps all.
If you’re unsure about what to do next, if you hem and haw, repeat yourself , change your mind, think out loud, speak too much or too fast, or appear befuddled, you’ll lose your students.
The first day of school isn’t just about setting the tone for your students. It’s also about setting the tone for yourself.

t: Why You Shouldn't Let Your Students Decide The Class Rules the-class-rules/
q: Allowing students to come up with the class rules is a common strategy.
Well, the problem with the strategy is that it can undermine your leadership presence.
You see, if in any way you communicate that you’re in partnership with your students when determining the direction of your classroom, it will weaken your authority.
This view of teacher as partner tends to be especially problematic with difficult students, who are quick to fill any void you leave them.
Having a teacher students trust to be at the helm from morning bell to dismissal has a calming effect on the tone and tenor of your classroom.
The truth is, you and your students have distinctly different responsibilities. Problems large and small arise when those responsibilities become confused or intertwined.

By presenting your rules as non-negotiable boundaries that you put into place for the express purpose of protecting their right to learn and enjoy school, you establish yourself as a compassionate leader who puts their interests first.
